title: Weight Columns
context: Grade 4, and the length columns again with one joining number. An adult sees the column work repeated. What is actually being taught is that grams take three places beside kilograms whatever their number. Whole kilograms are written with three zeros in the grams column before anything can be taken from them, as the page's Example 14 does. The last exercise question asks who weighs more and how much more, and the answer is two things, the heavier one and the difference; the book's own answer key gives both.

writeup.why: Add and take away weights in kilograms and grams, keeping three places for the grams, and answer which is heavier and by how much.
writeup.look: A kilograms and grams frame in the middle, a shelf of tagged bags at the left, and a balance with a two-blank answer card at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Weight Columns' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns worked against the two columns in the frame, grams and kilograms, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column's answer lands and the second fixed at two. On the first phase it counts the bags entered against the bags waiting, and on the fourth the answer card is counted as a third step, so the second number reads three. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The bag shelf stands at the left of the working area, 240 by 500 at 64,214, holding up to five bags, each with a weight tag in kilograms and grams or in grams alone. The column frame stands in the middle, 510 by 380 at 324,214: a kilograms column at the left headed kg, a grams column at the right headed g and cut into exactly three digit boxes, a near-black line between them, and the joining sign over the frame reading a thousand. A bag dragged to the frame drops its weight into a row one digit to a box, each digit sliding down into the column it belongs to; a tag in grams alone sends its last three digits into the grams boxes and the rest into the kilograms. Up to three rows, then a rule, then the answer row. Carry weights ride in a row over the kilograms column. Adding works the grams first, and each full thousand grams gathers into one deep blue kilogram weight that rises over the kilograms column, while what is left goes down as three digits. Taking away starts at the grams too. When the grams on top are fewer than the grams below, or read zero zero zero, the grams column stays shut and the break control, 220 by 56 at 324,610, lights over the kilograms on top. Break strikes them through, writes one less above in amber, and opens one kilogram weight into a thousand grams, drawn as ten green bars of a hundred grams, which join the grams on top, rewritten above them in amber. At the right the balance stands, 290 by 260 at 850,214, holding two bags, one on each pan. It tips toward the heavier bag as soon as both are on, before anything is worked. The answer card stands under it, 290 by 150 at 850,500, with two blanks, which bag is heavier and by how much, and it will not close while either blank is empty. On a take-away told as a story, the answer slot's label names what the question asks for, such as left in the sack. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across and has no dot key. The answer slot is a two-part measure, kilograms and then three grams boxes, with the unit names printed beside them. On the fourth phase the answer card's first blank takes one of two keys, each naming a bag by what is in it, and its second takes the measure. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green: metres beside kilometres, centimetres beside metres, millimetres, grams and millilitres. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that fills an empty place of the smaller unit is grey. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape, and the mark where a reading is taken, are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket, strike line, table rule and panel edge, is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, and a count by the slot that names what is counted, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in the smaller unit's places is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A figure that goes down by one when a unit is broken is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. No measure in two units is written as a decimal anywhere on the stage. The grams column keeps exactly three boxes whatever the number of grams. A kilogram weight opened by the break control is exactly a thousand grams, and a carried one is gathered from exactly a thousand. The balance judges the whole weight of each bag and tips before anything is worked, so the frame's answer can be checked against it, and once the difference is worked, a weight of exactly that much can be dropped onto the lighter bag's pan.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last sum or difference the child worked in the frame, and the balance with its answer card filled in.

phases.win: both weights stand in the frame with every grams box filled
phases.does: drops each bag's weight into the frame, filling every grams box
phases.goal: beside kilograms, grams take three places, so a short number of grams is written with zeros in front
phases.says: The grams column has three boxes. How is a two-digit number of grams written?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write 16 kg 5 g and 16 kg 50 g in columns. What goes in each grams column?
phases.feels: the grams get three boxes whatever their number, and a short number waits behind a zero
phases.hands: Draw two columns on the board headed kg and g, with three boxes under the g. Write 2 kg 350 g in the frame, then ask the class to write 1 kg 68 g under it. Let anyone who writes 680 show where the six and the eight went, and fill the hundreds box with a zero. Then write a weight in grams alone, 4070 g, and split it into the columns, its last three digits under the grams.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many grams boxes are there? Second rung, the phase's: which places does this number of grams fill? Third rung: the tag is cut to a single-digit number of grams, and the child fills all three boxes before the longer tag comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: digits are written from the left, and the first box is where writing begins.
wrong.move: types the sixty-eight grams of thirty-two kilograms sixty-eight grams into the first two grams boxes, so the row reads six hundred and eighty grams.
wrong.screen: the row is read back aloud as it stands, six hundred and eighty grams, more than half a kilogram, and its bag is drawn heavier than the tag beside it says. The six and the eight slide one box to the right, and a grey zero drops into the hundreds box at full size, zero six eight. The child's row stays drawn above the new one, nothing marked.

wrong.why: seventy has two digits and the grams have three boxes, so a zero is added at the end, where zeros usually go.
wrong.move: reads a tag of four thousand and seventy grams as four kilograms seven hundred grams, putting the seven in the first grams box.
wrong.screen: the tag's four digits slide down into the frame in the columns they stand in: the four under the kilograms, and zero, seven, zero into the three grams boxes, the first zero grey at full size. The grams are counted out beside the frame as seven bars of ten grams, where the child's seven hundred would need seven bars of a hundred. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the frame with two tagged bags waiting, one with a two-digit number of grams
phases.soWhat: Beside kilograms the grams take three places. A zero holds each place a short number of grams leaves empty.

phases.win: a kilogram weight rides over the kilograms column, and the sum stands with fewer than a thousand grams
phases.does: adds the grams, carries a kilogram weight, writes what is left, then adds the kilograms
phases.goal: each full thousand grams is carried as one kilogram
phases.says: The grams make more than a thousand. What is written, and what is carried?
phases.check: Add 18 kg 650 g and 24 kg 575 g. What is written in the grams column, and what is carried?
phases.feels: a thousand grams are too many for three boxes, so they become one kilogram and move across
phases.hands: Weigh two bags of rice on a kitchen scale and write both weights in columns. Add the grams first. When the grams come to more than a thousand, ask how many whole kilograms that is, write what is left in three places, and carry one kilogram. Put both bags on the scale together and compare its reading with the sum.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do the grams add up to? Second rung, the phase's: is that a thousand or more? Third rung: the frame is cut to two weights whose grams make just over a thousand, and the child carries before the larger sum comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the grams sum is one number, and splitting a number that has just been made feels wrong.
wrong.move: writes all of one thousand two hundred and forty-five in the grams column, and gets seventy-five kilograms and a four-digit number of grams.
wrong.screen: the grams sum shows one thousand two hundred and forty-five, and a thousand of those grams gather into one deep blue kilogram weight that rises over the kilograms, leaving two hundred and forty-five below. The child's four digits are laid over the three grams boxes and the first has no box to stand in. The kilograms are added again with the carried weight, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a hundred joins metres and centimetres, and that number is easy to reach for when the joining sign is passed over.
wrong.move: carries twelve kilograms and writes forty-five grams, splitting the sum at a hundred as for centimetres.
wrong.screen: the joining sign lights, a thousand, and the grams are laid out as weights: one kilogram's worth, a thousand grams, and two hundred and forty-five more. Twelve kilograms would need twelve thousand grams. One kilogram weight rises, and the child's eighty-seven kilograms forty-five grams stays in the slot beside seventy-six kilograms two hundred and forty-five grams.

wrong.why: once the grams are written the grams column looks finished, and the carried weight is easy to leave behind.
wrong.move: carries the kilogram but forgets to add it, and writes seventy-five kilograms two hundred and forty-five grams.
wrong.screen: the carried kilogram weight over the kilograms column glows, and the kilograms are added again with it travelling down into the sum: forty-six and twenty-nine make seventy-five, and one more makes seventy-six. The child's answer stays in the slot beside the new sum.

phases.screen: two weights in the frame whose grams add up to more than a thousand
phases.soWhat: Add the grams first. Each full thousand grams is carried as one kilogram, and only the grams left are written.

phases.win: the kilogram opens into a thousand grams, the kilograms go down by one, and the grams can be taken away
phases.does: opens one kilogram into a thousand grams and takes away the grams, then the kilograms
phases.goal: from zero grams, one kilogram is broken into a thousand grams
phases.says: No grams on top. Open one kilogram. How many grams does it give?
phases.check: A sack holds 25 kg of flour and 9 kg 350 g is used. How much flour is left in the sack?
phases.feels: with no grams on top, the opened kilogram makes all of them, and the kilograms pay for it
phases.hands: Write 20 kg on the board and write zero zero zero under the grams, as the chapter's worked take-away from a truck's load does. Ask the class to take 6 kg 250 g away. There are no grams on top, so break one kilogram: strike through the twenty, write nineteen above it, and write a thousand above the zeros. Take the grams, then the kilograms, and say the answer as what is left.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many grams are on top? Second rung, the phase's: where can grams come from when there are none? Third rung: the frame is cut to one kilogram, written with zero zero zero, and a few grams below, and the child opens it before the larger take-away comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: with nothing on top in the grams column, the grams below look as if there is nothing to take them from, so they come down as they are.
wrong.move: writes the four hundred and eighty grams from the bottom line straight down, and gets twenty-three kilograms four hundred and eighty grams for thirty-five kilograms less twelve kilograms four hundred and eighty grams.
wrong.screen: the grams column stays shut over the grey zeros, and the child's four hundred and eighty is written small beside it. The break control then strikes through thirty-five and writes thirty-four above it, and one kilogram weight opens into a thousand grams, ten bars of a hundred, over the zeros. Four hundred and eighty is taken from the thousand, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the thousand grams are the part that gets written, and the kilogram they came from is easy to forget to take off.
wrong.move: breaks a kilogram into a thousand grams but leaves the thirty-five kilograms as they were, and gets twenty-three kilograms five hundred and twenty grams.
wrong.screen: the thirty-five on top is lit with nothing struck through it, beside a thousand grams that came from nowhere, and the top weight's bag is drawn a kilogram heavier than its tag. The thirty-five is then struck through and thirty-four written above it, the take-away runs again, and the child's answer stays in the slot a kilogram too heavy.

wrong.why: both weights stand in a story about one sack, and adding is the first thing tried with two numbers.
wrong.move: adds the twelve kilograms four hundred and eighty grams sold to the thirty-five kilograms in the sack, and writes forty-seven kilograms four hundred and eighty grams for what is left.
wrong.screen: the sack is drawn with its thirty-five kilograms, and the weight sold is lifted out of it as a bag of its own, so the sack left is plainly lighter. The child's sum is drawn as a sack beside it, heavier than the full sack was. The answer slot's label, left in the sack, lights, and the take-away runs in the frame.

phases.screen: a weight of whole kilograms with zero zero zero in its grams column, and a weight with grams to take away
phases.soWhat: To take grams from zero grams, break one kilogram into a thousand grams. The kilograms on top go down by one, and the grams on top become a thousand.

phases.win: the heavier bag and the difference fill the two blanks, and the card closes
phases.does: reads which way the balance tips, takes the lighter weight from the heavier in the frame, and fills both blanks
phases.goal: a question that asks which is heavier and by how much needs two answers
phases.says: Which bag is heavier? Now how much heavier? Fill both blanks.
phases.check: One box weighs 8 kg 450 g and another 8 kg 45 g. Which is heavier, and by how much?
phases.feels: the balance already knows which bag is heavier; the frame finds out by how much
phases.hands: Put two bags of different weights on a pan balance, or weigh each on a kitchen scale, and ask which is heavier before anything is written. Write both weights, compare the kilograms first, and take the lighter from the heavier. Then ask the whole question again, which is heavier and by how much, and let the class answer both parts aloud.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which way does the balance tip? Second rung, the phase's: what does the question ask for, one thing or two? Third rung: the bags are cut to two whose kilograms differ and whose grams are both zero, and the child fills both blanks before the larger pair comes back. The bag keys and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the grams are the bigger number on the tags, and the eye goes to the biggest number.
wrong.move: chooses thirteen kilograms eight hundred and seventy-five grams as heavier than fourteen kilograms ninety grams, because eight hundred and seventy-five is more than ninety.
wrong.screen: the balance, tipped since both bags went on, is lit: the pan holding fourteen kilograms ninety grams hangs lower. The kilograms are compared first, fourteen against thirteen, and they decide it. The take-away runs with a kilogram broken, and the difference comes to two hundred and fifteen grams, the child's choice staying on the card beside it.

wrong.why: working out the difference is the long part, and its answer feels like the whole answer.
wrong.move: writes two hundred and fifteen grams and stops, without saying which bag is heavier.
wrong.screen: the card's first blank, which bag is heavier, stays empty and pulses, and the card will not close. The balance's lower pan is lit, and the child's two hundred and fifteen grams stays in the second blank, waiting for the first.

wrong.why: with the zeros passed over, the two tags look alike, and the kilograms are equal.
wrong.move: says twenty-one kilograms seventy grams and twenty-one kilograms seven hundred grams weigh the same, because both show twenty-one and a seven.
wrong.screen: the balance tips toward the second bag. The grams slide into their three boxes, zero seven zero and seven zero zero, and with the kilograms equal, the grams decide it. The difference comes to six hundred and thirty grams, and the child's answer stays on the card beside it.

phases.screen: two bags on the balance, and the answer card with both blanks empty
phases.soWhat: As weights are written, with fewer than a thousand grams, compare the kilograms first and the grams only when the kilograms are equal. Answer both parts: which is heavier, and by how much.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment a weight of exactly the difference is dropped onto the lighter bag's pan. The beam, tipped since the bags went on, lifts, wobbles and settles dead level, and the two pans hang side by side at one height. Take the weight off and the beam tips back. It can be tried with any two bags as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two tagged bags wait on the shelf, one with a two-digit number of grams, and the frame is empty down to its rule. On the second two weights already stand in the frame whose grams will add up past a thousand, the carry row empty. On the third the top line is a weight of whole kilograms with zero zero zero in its grams boxes, above a weight with grams, and the grams column is shut. On the fourth two bags hang on the balance, already tipped, and the answer card's two blanks are empty. The running count at the top left holds the columns worked against the columns in the frame, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the short tag, or the grams column, or the break control, or the answer card, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many boxes the grams take. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two or three weights added or taken away, with the carry weights, the break control and the balance open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on three places for grams, carrying a kilogram, borrowing a kilogram from zero grams, and saying which is heavier and by how much.
voiceLines: Bags with weight tags and a frame. How many boxes do the grams take?
The grams column has three boxes. How is a two-digit number of grams written?
The grams make more than a thousand. What is written, and what is carried?
No grams on top. Open one kilogram. How many grams does it give?
Which bag is heavier? Now how much heavier? Fill both blanks.
A new pair of bags. Read both tags before anything is added or taken.
Free play. Any weights in the frame, with the carry, the break and the balance open.
Read the question again, fill all three grams boxes, and work the grams first.
Every gram in its three places, every thousand carried or broken, and every question answered in full.

observations.why: The last three digits of four thousand and seventy are the grams left over after the whole kilograms, and seventy fills only the tens and the ones.
observations.soWhat: Beside kilograms the grams take three places, so seventy grams are written zero seven zero, and a zero holds the hundreds.
observations.observe: Four thousand and seventy grams dropped in as four kilograms and zero seven zero, the zero in the hundreds box at full size.

observations.why: A thousand grams are one kilogram, so they belong with the kilograms and cannot stay in three boxes.
observations.soWhat: Each full thousand grams is carried as one kilogram, and only the grams left are written.
observations.observe: Each time the grams passed a thousand, one kilogram weight rose over the kilograms and only what was left went down.

observations.why: There were no grams on top for it to join, so its thousand grams were all there was.
observations.soWhat: To take grams from zero grams, break one kilogram into a thousand grams. The kilograms on top go down by one.
observations.observe: From zero zero zero, the opened kilogram alone made the grams on top, a thousand.

observations.why: The question asked two things, which bag and how much, and a difference on its own says only how much.
observations.soWhat: With each weight written with fewer than a thousand grams, compare the kilograms first and the grams only when the kilograms are equal. Then answer both parts.
observations.observe: The balance tipped toward the heavier bag before any working, and the card would not close on the difference alone.

source_tool.description: A kilograms and grams column frame fills the middle of the stage, the grams column fixed at three boxes and a joining sign over it reading a thousand. Bags with weight tags wait on a shelf at the left and drop their weights into the rows, a short number of grams going in with zeros in front, so forty-five grams goes in as zero four five. Adding runs the grams column first; each full thousand grams becomes one kilogram weight carried over the kilograms column, and what is left is written below. Taking away starts at the grams too. When the grams on top are fewer than the grams below, or there are no grams on top at all, a break control opens one kilogram weight into a thousand grams: the kilograms on top go down by one and the grams on top grow by a thousand. A balance at the right holds two bags. It tips toward the heavier one before anything is worked, comparing kilograms first and grams only when the kilograms are equal, and an answer card under it has two blanks, which is heavier and by how much, and will not close while either blank is empty.
source_tool.art_direction: Tagged bags, a column frame, a balance / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a workbench with a tray of everyday things, a fifteen centimetre ruler, a ladder of units, a column frame with a unit switch, a pan balance with iron weights, a tap, jugs, glasses, jars, bottles and a tank.

A ruler is drawn as the page draws it: a long tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen, and a first tick carrying the unit name and no numeral. That first tick is the zero mark and lights as one.
Every measure is written with its unit named, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, as in 4 km 66 m. A measure in two units is never written as a decimal on any stage.

The smaller unit's places are fixed boxes: three beside kilometres, kilograms and litres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres. A zero filling one of those boxes is drawn at full size and weight and is never dimmed or dropped.

A number that joins two units is shown beside them wherever the child works with them: ten between millimetres and centimetres, a hundred between centimetres and metres, and a thousand between metres and kilometres, grams and kilograms, and millilitres and litres. Weight and capacity carry one number only, a thousand.
What is left after dividing is drawn in its own slot in the smaller unit, at full strength, and it is never folded into the quotient.

A larger unit broken to borrow is drawn as exactly the joining number of smaller pieces: ten pieces for a centimetre, a hundred for a metre, and a thousand for a kilometre, a kilogram or a litre, the thousand drawn as ten bars of a hundred.
No count, reading or result is shown before the child makes it. A jar count appears only once the pouring is done, and a reading only once the object is laid.
Every word on the stage says weight, the vocabulary box's word, for how heavy a thing is.
A container whose capacity is shown is drawn full to its brim.
Two measures being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a bar, a weight or a liquid the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that pads the smaller unit's places, as in zero seven five, is grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded, because it is holding a place. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape and the mark where a reading is taken are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket and table rule, is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because each unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, and a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the question again, fill all three grams boxes, and work the grams first.
voice.onNext: A new pair of bags. Read both tags before anything is added or taken.
voice.opening: Bags with weight tags and a frame. How many boxes do the grams take?
voice.onFinish: Every gram in its three places, every thousand carried or broken, and every question answered in full.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any weights in the frame, with the carry, the break and the balance open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After packets have been weighed on a kitchen scale and their weights written in kilograms and grams. The tool holds the grams to three boxes and tips a balance before the difference is worked. Its answer card asks for the heavier one as well as the amount.

answer_key.rule: Beside kilograms, grams take three places, and a short number of grams is written with zeros in front, so 45 g is 045. Add or take away the grams first. Each full thousand grams is carried as one kilogram. When the grams on top are fewer than the grams below, one kilogram is broken into a thousand grams. The kilograms on top go down by one and the grams on top grow by a thousand. A weight of whole kilograms is written with 000 in the grams column. To say which of two weights is heavier, compare the kilograms first, and the grams only when the kilograms are equal. A question that asks which is heavier and by how much needs both answers.
answer_key.wrong: The balance tips again, the grams column is redrawn with its three boxes, and the kilogram weight is opened into a thousand grams once more. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Beside kilograms, grams take three places, so 48 g is written 048.
Add the kilograms: 26 and 13 make 39. The sum is 39 kg 753 g.
items.question: Add 26 kg 48 g and 13 kg 705 g in columns.
items.checkpoint: Grams take three places beside kilograms, and zeros fill the places in front of a short number of grams.
items.misconception: Writing 48 g under the hundreds and tens of 705, which turns it into 480 g.

steps: 1487 g is 1 kg 487 g, so write 487 and carry 1 kg.
Add the kilograms with the carry: 58 and 34 and 1 make 93. The sum is 93 kg 487 g.
items.question: Add 58 kg 675 g and 34 kg 812 g.
items.checkpoint: Each full thousand grams is carried as one kilogram.
items.misconception: Writing 1487 in the grams column, or carrying at a hundred.

steps: Write 60 kg as 60 kg 000 g, with three zeros in the grams column.
There are no grams on top, so break one kilogram into a thousand grams: 59 kg 1000 g. Then 1000 less 350 is 650.
59 less 18 is 41, so 41 kg 650 g of mangoes is left in the crate.
items.answer: 41 kg 650 g of mangoes is left in the crate
items.question: A crate holds 60 kg of mangoes. 18 kg 350 g of them are sold. How much is left in the crate?
items.checkpoint: From zero grams, one kilogram is broken into a thousand grams, and the kilograms go down by one.
items.misconception: Taking 0 from 350 and writing 350 g, which gives 42 kg 350 g.

steps: Compare the kilograms first: 21 is more than 17, so the second suitcase is heavier.
Take away in columns: 21 kg 045 g less 17 kg 280 g. 45 g is less than 280 g, so break one kilogram: 20 kg 1045 g.
1045 less 280 is 765, and 20 less 17 is 3. The second suitcase is heavier by 3 kg 765 g.
items.answer: The second suitcase is heavier, by 3 kg 765 g
items.question: One suitcase weighs 17 kg 280 g and another weighs 21 kg 45 g. Which is heavier, and by how much?
items.checkpoint: Compare the kilograms first; a question that asks which and how much needs both answers.
items.misconception: Choosing the first suitcase because 280 is more than 45, or giving 3 kg 765 g without saying which suitcase is heavier.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How is 7 g written in the grams column beside kilograms?
12 kg 90 g is written in columns. What goes in the grams column?
Add 34 kg 760 g and 27 kg 385 g.
items.final_answer: 62 kg 145 g. The grams make 1145, so write 145 and carry 1 kg

items.question: A shop sold 15 kg 640 g of flour, 22 kg 75 g of rice and 9 kg 480 g of sugar. What total weight did it sell?
items.final_answer: 47 kg 195 g. The grams make 1195, so write 195 and carry 1 kg

items.question: Take 7 kg 425 g from 20 kg.
items.final_answer: 12 kg 575 g. Write 20 kg as 20 kg 000 g and break one kilogram into a thousand grams

items.question: Take 36 kg 780 g from 81 kg 215 g.
items.final_answer: 44 kg 435 g. Break one kilogram: 80 kg 1215 g, and 1215 less 780 is 435

items.question: A bag of potatoes weighs 9 kg 150 g and a bag of onions weighs 11 kg 40 g. Which bag is heavier, and by how much?
items.final_answer: The bag of onions is heavier, by 1 kg 890 g

items.question: Parcel A weighs 12 kg 60 g and parcel B weighs 12 kg 600 g. Which parcel is heavier, and by how much?
items.final_answer: Parcel B is heavier, by 540 g. The kilograms are equal, and 600 g is more than 060 g

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: bags with weight tags that drop their weights into the rows
kilograms and grams, with the grams fixed at three boxes
one kilogram carried for each full thousand grams
opens one kilogram weight into a thousand grams
tips toward the heavier of two bags, kilograms first and grams only when the kilograms are equal
two blanks, which is heavier and by how much

teaching_notes: Weigh two or three packets on a kitchen scale before the tool is opened and write each weight in kilograms and grams. Example 13 says to write forty-five grams as zero four five. Example 14 writes zero zero zero under the grams of five hundred kilograms before it borrows. Both are the three places that grams take beside kilograms. Every borrow in this topic breaks one kilogram into a thousand grams, and the kilograms go down by one. In Exercise 11.4 several additions have grams that come to more than a thousand, and two subtractions take away from whole kilograms. Its last question asks who weighs more and how much more, which is two answers, and the book's key gives both; do not accept the difference on its own. To say which weight is heavier, compare the kilograms first and look at the grams only when the kilograms are equal. Say weight throughout.
generation_prompt: Build a column tool for weights on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A two-column frame headed kg and g fills the middle of the working area, the g column fixed at exactly three digit boxes, with a joining sign over the frame reading a thousand. A shelf at the left holds bags with weight tags; a bag dragged to the frame drops its weight into a row, one digit to a box, a short number of grams entering with zeros in front drawn at full size. Adding works the g column first; each full thousand grams becomes one kilogram weight carried over the kg column, and the rest is written below. Taking away also starts at the g column; when the grams on top are fewer than the grams below, or read 000, the frame waits, and a break control opens one kilogram weight into a thousand grams drawn as ten bars of a hundred, the kg on top going down by one and the g on top growing by a thousand. At the right a balance holds two bags and tips toward the heavier before anything is worked, judging by kilograms first and by grams only when the kilograms are equal. Under it an answer card has two blanks, which is heavier and by how much, and it will not close while either is empty. Every label says weight. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fill all three grams boxes. Work the grams first. Carry a kilogram for each thousand grams. Open a kilogram when the grams are too few. Say which is heavier, and by how much.
